\section[gaudium, gaudiī]{gaudium, gaudiī — joy}

\label{lesson:LA-C69-gaudium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for thirst, then the Latin for care.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gaudium, gaudiī}
\textbf{gaudium, gaudiī} — \textquotedblleft{}joy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gaudium} is built on \emph{gaudeō}, \textquotedblleft{}to rejoice\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1). English \emph{joy} comes from its plural through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[īra, īrae]{īra, īrae — anger}

\label{lesson:LA-C69-ira}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for care, then the Latin for joy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: īra, īrae}
\textbf{īra, īrae} — \textquotedblleft{}anger\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{ire} and \emph{irate}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{īra} is probably inherited, from a Proto-Indo-European root \emph{*h1eysh2-}, \textquotedblleft{}to fall upon, to act sharply\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[timor, timōris]{timor, timōris — fear}

\label{lesson:LA-C69-timor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for joy, then the Latin for anger.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: timor, timōris}
\textbf{timor, timōris} — \textquotedblleft{}fear\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{timid}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{timor} is built on \emph{timeō}, \textquotedblleft{}to fear\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), with the ending \emph{-or}, \textquotedblleft{}a state\textquotedblright{}. Where \emph{timeō} comes from is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[laetus, laeta, laetum]{laetus, laeta, laetum — happy, glad}

\label{lesson:LA-C69-laetus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for anger, then the Latin for fear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: laetus, laeta, laetum}
\textbf{laetus, laeta, laetum} — \textquotedblleft{}happy, glad\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{laetus} has no sure origin; no proposal is generally accepted. Lewis \& Short give it the sense \textquotedblleft{}rich, fertile\textquotedblright{} for crops and fields.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[trīstis, trīste]{trīstis, trīste — sad}

\label{lesson:LA-C69-tristis}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for fear, then the Latin for happy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: trīstis, trīste}
\textbf{trīstis, trīste} — \textquotedblleft{}sad\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{trīstis} has no sure origin. Lewis \& Short call it doubtful; EtymDB 2.1 records a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European \emph{*treystis}, \textquotedblleft{}in a bad mood\textquotedblright{}, but the link is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}
